The Secret to Better Gravy Is Already In Your Pantry

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It only takes a splash to give homemade gravy the rich, savory flavor you're after.
  • According to recent reports, there are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy.
  • Making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It only takes a splash to give homemade gravy the rich, savory flavor you're after.

According to recent reports, there are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy. Everyone seems to have a preferred method, a secret ingredient or a little trick they’ve been using for years. My mom has always sworn by Kitchen Bouquet, a seasoning sauce that gives gravy a little color and kick of flavor. I’m fairly certain she’s had the same bottle since the Reagan administration, and that it only comes out of the cupboard on Thanksgiving.

Making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky. Even with plenty of turkey drippings and a well-made stock, sometimes it needs a little something extra. Over the years, I’ve experimented with all sorts of ways to give my gravy more flavor, but the one I come back to every time is an ingredient I always have in my pantry.

I’ve been adding a splash of soy sauce to my gravy for years, and it’s one of those little tricks that makes a noticeable difference without anyone being able to put their finger on why.

Industry observers note that soy sauce is rich in umami, the deeply savory flavor that makes foods like mushrooms, Parmesan cheese and the golden crust of a steak so satisfying. Adding a little soy sauce to gravy enhances those same savory flavors, giving it a richness that might otherwise require a longer cooking time. It doesn’t make your gravy taste like soy sauce, provided you use a light hand. It just makes it taste more like really good gravy.

Recent findings suggest that worcestershire sauce is another popular addition that works for much the same reason, bringing its own combination of savory flavor, acidity and a hint of sweetness. I’ve tried plenty of different additions over the years, and while they all have their merits, soy sauce remains my favorite. I love the depth it brings without competing with the flavors of the turkey and stock.

In a recent development, the trick with soy sauce is knowing when to add it and, perhaps most importantly, when to stop. You’re not trying to introduce a newly introduced flavor to your gravy so much as coax a little more out of what’s already there. If someone can identify soy sauce in the finished product, you’ve probably been a bit too generous.

Industry observers note that I always add mine at the end, once the gravy has thickened and I’m happy with the consistency. Start with about a teaspoon for every two cups of gravy, stir it in, and give it a taste. Depending on the stock and drippings you’ve used, that may be all you need. If not, add a little more, tasting as you go.

One thing worth remembering is that soy sauce is salty. Very salty, in fact, so save your final seasoning adjustments until after you’ve added it. This is particularly important if you’re using store-bought stock, which may already contain plenty of sodium. Reduced-sodium soy sauce is an option, too, but I generally use the regular stuff and adjust accordingly.

Industry observers note that and don’t save this trick for Thanksgiving! It works beautifully in beef and chicken gravy, too, especially when the pan drippings aren’t quite as flavorful as you’d hoped. A splash of soy sauce won’t make up for a badly made gravy, but it can do an impressive amount of work for an otherwise perfectly respectable one.

Industry observers note that have you used soy sauce in gravy before? Let us know in the comments below!

#43081. Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (652 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

According to recent reports, IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

#43080. Cheese Dreams

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you.
  • For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters.
  • After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →.

It has been revealed that massive Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Rao’s Made-for-Home Meat Lasagna, 9-oz.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

Industry observers note that we cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

Half a can of pumpkin leftover pumpkin may not be enough for another pie, but you can definitely put it to use in other fall recipes.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a proposal. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

Fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

These are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

The pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

According to recent reports, best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

And there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the upcoming Congress.

Industry observers note that the conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a initiative to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., mentioned the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

In a recent development, “I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he mentioned, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sources indicate that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

Industry observers note that no challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators remarked. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer remarked, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

It has been revealed that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., stated voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

According to recent reports, “The cost of living defeated us,” Paul remarked. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer mentioned.

How We Brought a Taste of Maine to Bon Appétit LIVE

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.
  • The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

The class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

After years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Sources indicate that speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in fresh equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an key part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in Newly introduced Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”.

In a recent development, A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette mentioned that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

It has been revealed that most crucial, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you're wrapping up Thanksgiving dinner, you're probably looking for a tasty drink and a little something sweet to finish the meal. But why not have both at the same time with a dessert cocktail? This boozy Turkeytini has all you need to complete your Thanksgiving feast with the decadent blend of creamy Baileys Irish cream, chocolate liqueur, Kahlúa, and bourbon.

Hot tip: Make sure to shake the cocktail for a good 20 seconds or more to get it homogeneous and frothy. This is the secret to getting a smooth drink without any curdling or separation. This recipe makes one drink, but feel free to increase all the ingredients to make a substantial batch—plus, the more Reese's, the better!

The garnish:It's entirely optional, but I took a note from our Oreo turkeys and made an adorable Reese's turkey as a garnish for this drink. Here's how you do it: Dot the back of 2 candy eyes with melted chocolate. Place on a Reese’s Thins cup. Use more chocolate to attach the orange part of a candy corn as the beak. For feathers, halve another cup and attach to the back with more chocolate. I promise it will make your drink all the more delicious (and adorable).

Maple-Sausage Breakfast Casserole

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

According to recent reports, cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Recent findings suggest that pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

HexClad Bakeware Review: This Set Is So Sturdy and Nonstick, I’m Ditching Parchment Paper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
  • Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

As an avid baker, I've been waiting for such a sturdy set.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Serious bakers will appreciate the hefty, high-quality materials in this 6-piece set. It's also gloriously nonstick.

When I got married a few years ago, I put a cohesive bakeware set on my registry to replace years of mismatched Goodwill finds. While it worked well for a few months, within a year it began to show serious signs of wear and tear. Baked-on grease stains, rust spots and even warping had me in the market for a latest bakeware set much sooner than I expected.

According to recent reports, so, when I heard that my favorite cookware brand was releasing a bakeware set promising a sturdy, nonstick experience, I jumped at the chance to test it. Here’s everything you need to know about the fresh HexClad bakeware line, including my honest thoughts after two months of testing.

HexClad’s fresh hybrid bakeware set features six core pieces:.

In a recent development, it merges the benefits of stainless steel and nonstick into one easy-to-clean package. HexClad’s “hybrid technology” combines hexagonal steel peaks with nonstick valleys to improve heat circulation and release after baking. In other words, this bakeware browns your food evenly without it sticking to the pan.

In a recent development, other features include ergonomic handles and a 2.5mm tri-ply construction to prevent warping. It’s also oven-safe up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit and dishwasher-safe. You can even use your favorite metal spatula or tongs without scratching the surface. And, like all HexClad cookware, it comes with a lifetime warranty against manufacturer’s defects.

According to recent reports, I’ll admit: I’m already a significant fan of HexClad. I reach for the brand’s skillets and knives daily, and I’ve hoped for years that they would release a bakeware line.

Sources indicate that so, when the offer to test the new set landed in my inbox, I couldn’t say no. But would it live up to the hype I’d built up in my head? I put all six pieces through the paces for two months to find out.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that like all HexClad products I’ve tried, the bakeware packaging experience is impeccable. The set arrived securely in one significant box, separated with foam. Each piece was also wrapped in a protective dust bag, which is a nice touch.

Immediately, I was awed by the construction of these pans. Just by touch, I could tell they were high quality. I grabbed my food scale to compare the weight of the HexClad pans to my go-to carbon steel pans. The HexClad options weighed more than twice as much as my existing bakeware. Talk about heft!

Now, some folks might not appreciate that extra weight—especially since the pans get even heavier when full of food. But as someone who often replaces her bakeware every few years due to warping or rusting, I’m excited for a sturdier option. I hope this is the last set of bakeware I ever need to order.

As a final step, I washed each piece and got ready to bake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

One of my favorite things to make with sourdough discard is a big loaf of focaccia bread, so that was a natural first test in the 13×9 HexClad pan. Focaccia dough is sticky, but a generous coating of olive oil helps prevent it from gluing to the pan. Still, after proofing and baking my bread as usual, I was impressed that the final product pulled slightly away from the pan’s edges, making it slide out with complete ease. The bottom and edges got nice and toasty brown, too.

Recent findings suggest that A few nights later, I used the same focaccia dough to make a focaccia pizza. Same sticky dough, made even stickier with tomato sauce, cheese and toppings. Plus, since it’s such a rich dish, I cut back on the amount of olive oil I used. Despite all the add-ons, this focaccia baked and released from the pan just as beautifully as the first loaf.

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that next, I made a chocolate layer cake with the 9-inch round cake pans. Now, I’m typically a ride-or-die parchment paper user. I find cutting out perfectly sized parchment circles a tedious task, but it’s worthwhile insurance against my cakes sticking. But to truly put the HexClad pans’ nonstick properties to the test, I skipped adding parchment and simply greased my pans with a little butter and flour.

After baking and 10 minutes of cooling came the moment of truth: Would it stick? Luckily, no! Both cakes released with minimal effort. I simply ran a butter knife around the rim of the cake before using the cooling rack to flip ’em out. It’s a good thing, too, because this was my dad’s birthday cake!

Katie Bandurski For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, my nonstick tests continued with the 8×8 square pan when I whipped up a batch of candy bar blondies. These blondies used an assortment of leftover Halloween candy, so I thought for sure the caramel ooze from a Baby Ruth bar would cause some complications. But nope! Even without parchment paper, treats slipped right out of the pan.

Industry observers note that but how does HexClad bakeware perform with healthier treats? For one final test, I baked a completely made-up “brownie” recipe with pumpkin seed butter, applesauce, molasses and cocoa. It was a gooey, chocolaty mess by the time I put it in the pan, yet it baked and released beautifully.

Finally, I put the baking sheet to the test.

Sources indicate that now, I already own the HexClad pizza steel, which I use almost daily. It’s my go-to for everything from frozen pizza to galettes to roasted broccoli, and I find that it works even better than an air fryer to yield crisp, golden brown bakes. I’ve stated on many occasions that it’s my all-time favorite piece of bakeware, especially for savory foods.

In a recent development, both the pizza steel and baking sheet utilize HexClad’s tri-ply construction with an aluminum core and TerraBond nonstick coating. The former is a jet black colorway, while the baking sheet is gray.

Recent findings suggest that across the board, I found the baking sheet could handle every task I threw its way—including roasting a spaghetti squash. Oftentimes, I find myself scrubbing for what feels like days after roasting squash and scouring off that sticky, burnt-on residue. The HexClad pan cleaned with a simple swipe from a damp paper towel.

Recent findings suggest that during testing, I found the bottoms and handles of the HexClad bakeware smudged a bit. After all, it is made of stainless steel. This didn’t bother me, and it was easy to clean by handwashing and drying it immediately. Over time, I may need to use a more abrasive regimen to clean stainless steel.

While the HexClad pans are very sturdy, you should still let them fully cool before washing. Don’t throw a hot pan directly in the sink. The pans are also dishwasher-safe, though handwashing is recommended. (And honestly, so easy thanks to the nonstick coating.).

Across the board, I’m impressed with the newly introduced HexClad bakeware line. I hope we see even more pieces in the future, like a muffin tin and loaf pan. Only time will tell exactly how it holds up, but from what I’ve experienced so far, this set really is designed to last a lifetime. (And I’ll be continuing to long-term test the set, and revision this review accordingly.).

Recent findings suggest that ready to take your bakes to the next level? This all-in-one set is great for beginners and pros alike.

You can shop the full 6-piece bakeware set on the HexClad website for $399. Select styles, like 2-pack sets of small and medium baking sheets, are also available.

Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, mentioned legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

Sources indicate that “Yes, absolutely,” she stated when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

It has been revealed that rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses unveiled a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

Sources indicate that the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack remarked she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

It has been revealed that “That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she remarked when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this glitch.”.

Leger Fernández noted if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

#43061. Tech Report: Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (831 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined.
  • It has been revealed that I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone.
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

It has been revealed that I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Recent findings suggest that imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

In a recent development, “Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” states Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”.

In a recent development, the pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Grace Natoli Sheldon for Taste of Home.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Recent findings suggest that poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

It has been revealed that if any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

Sources indicate that if the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

You should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

Turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can also be the star of dessert if you stretch your imagination enough. This idea first gained popularity on TikTok, using chocolate-dipped strawberries, marshmallows, pretzel rods, and melted chocolate to create these adorable little treats.

In a recent development, they're so simple to make: To make a leg, you spear two mini marshmallows with half a pretzel rod, then use kitchen shears to trim the edges into a long oval shape. Repeat for a second leg, then cut one mini marshmallow diagonally in half to make the wings. You'll stick these to the strawberry with a dab of melted chocolate (which acts as your glue), then let that sit to adhere. All that's left is a quick bath in melted chocolate.

Breaking: The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

Recent findings suggest that there are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef mentioned.

Sources indicate that ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee claims.

According to recent reports, consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

In a recent development, running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a latest planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee notes of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Recent findings suggest that ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

According to recent reports, “I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he states. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

#43058. Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (788 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious.
  • For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates.
  • Recent findings suggest that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Recent findings suggest that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

Industry observers note that personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

Recent findings suggest that the same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

According to recent reports, mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

According to recent reports, green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that california Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

According to recent reports, the race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

It has been revealed that the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

Recent findings suggest that in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

It has been revealed that the race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

It has been revealed that one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

It has been revealed that two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#43052. Industry News: How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1412 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • It has been revealed that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • Recent findings suggest that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

It has been revealed that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

Recent findings suggest that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

It has been revealed that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Sources indicate that be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

It has been revealed that because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

Industry observers note that if you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Sources indicate that kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

It has been revealed that most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

Industry observers note that in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

It has been revealed that secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

Sources indicate that you can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Recent findings suggest that need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

Industry observers note that in any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

Recent findings suggest that this is probably a temperature problem. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Sources indicate that another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with fresh reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

Dirty Spaghetti

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.
  • Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish!
  • Recent findings suggest that the key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

Recent findings suggest that the key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an crucial cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

Industry observers note that dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

It has been revealed that heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

Add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

Industry observers note that add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

Remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

In a recent development, the best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

Yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

Sources indicate that first, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

It has been revealed that you’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?
